levels.17.title: Same diagram, different drawing
levels.17.intro: We've numbered the particles: 1 and 2 come in, 3 and 4 go out. Are two different drawings two different diagrams? Decide what really matters.
levels.17.steps.same.prompt: Do A and B represent the same Feynman diagram?
levels.17.steps.same.diagrams.0.label: A
levels.17.steps.same.diagrams.1.label: B
levels.17.steps.same.options.yes.text: Yes: they connect the same particles to the same vertices
levels.17.steps.same.options.yes.feedbac: The shape of the drawing doesn't matter: only the topology does, that is, what connects to what.
levels.17.steps.same.options.no.text: No: in B the photon is tilted and curved
levels.17.steps.same.options.no.feedback: Geometry has no meaning. Moving vertices or curving lines doesn't change the diagram.
levels.17.steps.same.hints.0: Follow each number to its vertex.
levels.17.steps.same.hints.1: In both, 1 and 3 share a vertex, and so do 2 and 4.
levels.17.steps.different.prompt: And these two? Are they the same diagram?
levels.17.steps.different.options.no.tex: No: in C electron 1 shares a vertex with exit 4
levels.17.steps.different.options.no.fee: It changes which final particle is connected to each initial one: it's a different contribution.
levels.17.steps.different.options.yes.te: Yes: both have two vertices and a photon
levels.17.steps.different.options.yes.fe: Having the same pieces isn't enough: how they connect matters. In C the lines cross and 1 ends up at 4.
levels.17.steps.different.hints.0: Look at which exit particle 1 shares a vertex with in each drawing.
levels.17.steps.different.hints.1: In A, 1 goes with 3. In C, 1 goes with 4.
levels.17.success: You've discovered topology: a diagram is a network of connections, not a drawing.
levels.17.explanation.intuitive: Like on a subway map, you can stretch and bend the lines without changing anything, as long as the connections stay the same.
levels.17.explanation.scientific: Two diagrams are equivalent if there's a correspondence between their vertices that preserves the connections, the line types and the external particles. Topologically distinct diagrams are different contributions to the amplitude.
levels.17.explanation.math: The total amplitude is the sum over all topologically distinct diagrams: 𝓜 = Σ 𝓜_i. Counting the same diagram twice would give a wrong result.
levels.18.title: The other way
levels.18.intro: Electrons are identical: there's no way to know whether electron 1 ended up at exit 3 or exit 4. Nature takes both possibilities into account.
levels.18.steps.u.prompt: Above is the contribution you already know. Build the other tree-level contribution to e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻.
levels.18.steps.u.reference.label: Already known
levels.18.steps.u.hints.0: In the known one, 1 goes with 3 and 2 goes with 4. Try another pairing.
levels.18.steps.u.hints.1: Join 1 and 4 to one vertex, and 2 and 3 to the other. Then connect the vertices with a photon.
levels.18.success: You've found the crossed contribution (u channel). For identical particles, both stories count.
levels.18.explanation.intuitive: If you can't tell the electrons apart, you can't know which went where. Both possibilities contribute at once.
levels.18.explanation.scientific: Møller scattering has two tree-level diagrams: the t channel (1→3, 2→4) and the u channel (1→4, 2→3). The second exists because the final electrons are indistinguishable.
levels.18.explanation.math: 𝓜 = 𝓜_t − 𝓜_u. The negative relative sign comes from Fermi–Dirac statistics: swapping two identical fermions changes the sign of the amplitude.
levels.19.title: Bhabha: two stories
levels.19.intro: An electron and a positron can be deflected by exchanging a photon, as you've seen. But they have another option that two electrons don't.
levels.19.steps.s.prompt: Build the annihilation contribution (s channel): electron 1 and positron 2 meet at the same vertex.
levels.19.steps.s.reference.label: t channel (known)
levels.19.steps.s.hints.0: The two initial particles go to the left vertex; the final ones, to the right one.
levels.19.steps.s.hints.1: Between the two vertices you need a line that carries no charge.
levels.19.steps.meaning.prompt: In the diagram you've just built, what happens?
levels.19.steps.meaning.options.annihila: The pair annihilates into a virtual photon, which then creates a new pair
The initial pair disappears completely and a new pair is born from the virtual photon.
levels.19.steps.meaning.options.bounce.t: The electron and the positron bounce off without touching
levels.19.steps.meaning.options.bounce.f: That describes the t channel. Here they meet at the same vertex.
levels.19.steps.meaning.hints.0: Look at which particles share the left vertex.
levels.19.steps.meaning.hints.1: After that vertex only a photon remains.
levels.19.success: You've drawn two different stories for the same process.
levels.19.explanation.intuitive: Either they're deflected by exchanging a photon, or they turn into a photon and reappear. Both contribute to what we see.
levels.19.explanation.scientific: Bhabha scattering has two tree-level diagrams: scattering (t channel) and annihilation (s channel). At high energies, the s channel is the basis of e⁺e⁻ colliders such as LEP.
levels.19.explanation.math: 𝓜 = 𝓜_t − 𝓜_s, with propagators 1/t and 1/s, where s = (p₁ + p₂)² is the total centre-of-mass energy squared.
levels.20.title: Count the contributions
levels.20.intro: A physicist calculating a process has to find every diagram that contributes, not one more, not one less. Do the count.
levels.20.steps.moller.prompt: How many tree-level (two-vertex) diagrams contribute to e⁻e⁻ → e⁻e⁻?
levels.20.steps.moller.options.1.feedbac: Remember level 18: identical electrons give one more contribution.
levels.20.steps.moller.options.2.feedbac: Exactly: the direct one and the crossed one.
levels.20.steps.moller.options.3.feedbac: The s channel doesn't exist for two electrons. Why? You'll see next.
levels.20.steps.moller.hints.0: There are three ways to pair four particles at two vertices.
levels.20.steps.moller.hints.1: One of them violates charge conservation.
levels.20.steps.no-s.prompt: Why is there no s-channel diagram for two electrons?
levels.20.steps.no-s.options.charge.text: Two electrons have charge −2, and a photon has none: the arrow couldn't continue at the vertex
levels.20.steps.no-s.options.charge.feed: Two arrows would come into that vertex and none would leave.
levels.20.steps.no-s.options.touch.feedb: In Bhabha's s channel the electron and the positron do share a vertex. The problem is the charge.
levels.20.steps.no-s.hints.0: Imagine a vertex with both incoming electrons.
levels.20.steps.no-s.hints.1: How many arrows come in and how many go out?
levels.20.steps.bhabha.prompt: And how many tree-level diagrams contribute to e⁻e⁺ → e⁻e⁺?
levels.20.steps.bhabha.options.1.feedbac: In level 19 you built one more.
levels.20.steps.bhabha.options.2.feedbac: The u channel would join the initial electron with the final positron at a vertex: the arrows wouldn't flow.
levels.20.steps.bhabha.options.3.feedbac: The u channel is impossible here: it would violate charge conservation at the vertex.
levels.20.steps.bhabha.hints.1: Initial electron with final positron: is charge conserved?
levels.20.success: You're doing the first task of a real calculation: finding every diagram.
levels.20.explanation.intuitive: There are few ways to connect four particles with two vertices, and the rules rule some out. The ones left are all the possible stories.
levels.20.explanation.scientific: With four external particles there are three pairings (s, t, u). Charge conservation at the vertices removes some. Møller keeps t and u; Bhabha, s and t. This game's engine enumerates these diagrams automatically to check the levels.
levels.20.explanation.math: At order e², the total amplitude is the sum of the allowed diagrams with their relative signs. The cross-section is ∝ |Σ 𝓜_i|² and includes interference terms between diagrams.
